node.idea: With the pawn on g6 Black clears the way to fianchetto the bishop to g7, where it will rake the long diagonal from the corner straight through the centre toward White's queenside.
The bishop settles on g7 and immediately leans on the long diagonal; its first target is the knight on d4, the piece holding White's grip on the centre.

The bishop backs up the d4-knight and readies castling long — the sharp opposite-wings main line. Capturing on c6 instead would be a concession: Black recaptures toward the centre and the b-file opens against b2.

This is what keeps it an ACCELERATED Dragon: the knight comes to f6 before the d-pawn commits. Play the pawn to d6 now and White gets f3, transposing into a Main-Line Dragon; holding the pawn on its home square keeps the one-move central break in reserve.

A rule to burn in: once White's queen leaves its home square in a Dragon, look hard at the knight leap to g4. Trading that knight for the dark-squared bishop leaves the g7-bishop without a rival on its diagonal. The catch — after the leap the bishop can't step off e3, since the twice-attacked d4-knight would fall, so White's only try is to capture on c6 first.

With the concrete lines still murky, the soundest choice is to finish developing and castle. The pawn deliberately stays home: if White insists on a Main-Line Dragon setup, the central break in one move is the reward.

White castles long, and now the king and queen sit on the same file — that changes the whole assessment. The knight leap to g4 comes back on: after the capture on c6 and the bishop's move to d4, the bishop swings to h6 and pins the queen to the king. White blocks with f4, but then the e-pawn hits f4 and, with the pin freezing it, wins material.

The knight jumps in with a double point: it eyes the bishop on e3 and, with the queen no longer home, the whole h6-pin idea is live. The bishop still can't move — the d4-knight is attacked twice and would drop.

Recapturing toward the centre swings the b-file wide open, and with White castled long that file points straight at b2 — the attack writes itself. The c-pawn now becomes a battering ram against White's king cover.
There it is — the bishop swings to h6 and pins the queen to the king along the dark diagonal. The queen is nailed in place.

The crusher. The e-pawn strikes f4, and because the queen is pinned the pawn cannot capture back — it is as if f4 were not there — so the bishop on d4 falls and Black emerges a full piece up. Precision first, though: snatching with the bishop on f4 with check is the tempting error; after the king steps aside, taking on d4 lets White recapture and the f4-bishop is left hanging. Take on d4 first — the f4-pawn is not going anywhere.

This is the sting of the mainline: Black is often forced to push the pawn to e5, and the bishop drops to c5, shutting down the g7-bishop's diagonal. It takes much of the fun out of the Dragon, and White is considered better here.

node.idea: White develops the bishop to c4, aiming at f7 — the sharp Sozin-style setup. Black just keeps developing; depending on White's next move it will be castling, or d6, or sometimes d5 in one go.
Castling first, and deliberately NOT the pawn to d6 yet — holding it back preserves maximum flexibility. That reserve pays off if White castles, when the one-move d5 break becomes available.
The knight retreat to e2 is a poor choice — it steps off the strong d4-square passively and hands Black an immediate way to challenge in the centre.
The knight leaps to g4, harassing the e3-bishop — a move that can be genuinely nasty here, since the bishop has no comfortable square that keeps everything defended.

The queen swings to b6 — a garden-variety double attack, hitting the f2- and b2-pawns at once. It comes with risk, since the light-squared bishop is still at home, but the fork is real and White can only defend one pawn.
Grab it — the pawn on b2. The queen looks adventurous but it won't be trapped: the a3-square is a ready retreat and there are escape routes to spare, so this is simply a clean extra pawn.
The knight comes back from its loose post on g4 to the fine central square e5, hitting the c4-bishop as it arrives — its job on g4 is done, and e5 is a much sturdier home.
The pawn to g5 chases the bishop off the board's active diagonal altogether. Booting the strong piece unburdens the position and lets Black consolidate the extra material in peace.
Now the pawn to d6 is safe — e7 is well covered — so Black finally locks the centre without weakening the dark squares that a combined g6-and-e6 would have left soft.
The knight to g4 with check is crushing — it drives the exposed king onto the run into a mating net, and Black's attack, a pawn up already, simply finishes the game.

node.idea: The pawn to f3 is the Fantasy Variation — White keeps the big centre and plays for a rich, tactical middlegame rather than a theoretical duel.
The bishop to c4 trains on f7 and must stay on that diagonal — it is what keeps the pressure on f7 alive for the tactics to come.
The quiet pawn to c3 shores up d4, the pawn holding White's centre. If d4 ever falls, a black knight lands on the e5 outpost and White is in trouble, so the centre is secured first.

Rather than a caveman pawn storm, White improves the pieces: the knight to c4 eyes the bishop on d6 and the dark squares. Against opposite-side castling, a piece build-up is a valid, less committal plan.

node.idea: This is the Rubinstein French — Black gives up the centre with the capture on e4 for a rock-solid, if slightly passive, structure. It can arrive through the Tarrasch or the Nc3 move order, and every e4-player has to know how to handle it.
Trading on f6 reaches the main tabia of the line. From here White has five or six reasonable setups — g3, the classical Bd3 — but the one with the best modern reputation is coming.

The move is the pawn to c3, and it's easy to misread as purely positional. Yes, it reinforces d4 — but it also opens the d1-a4 diagonal, and the check on a4 is a major resource in these positions as long as Black's king sits on e8.
The bishop to e3 develops with a point — it leans on c5, and the real threat is simply to capture there. A developing move that also poses a concrete question is worth two.

Now the knight to e5 — the perfect moment to centralise it. The check on a4 would achieve nothing, since Black just plays the bishop to d7 and you've only helped him develop; the knight on e5 is the real prize.

Leaning toward the capture on c5 — into an endgame rather than a middlegame. It's not clearly the best, but it poses Black an immediate dilemma: take on e3 and enter the ending, or not. Posing problems has value of its own.

Queens come off and the pawn recaptures on e3. Black has lost the right to castle, and while White's e-pawns are doubled, the c5-b4-c3 wall is about to strangle any queenside counterplay — an excellent structure to grind from.
Start with the knight to c4 — the move you want anyway. It's flexible, it discourages the bishop coming to f6 because the knight to d6 arrives with tempo, and it keeps every option open.
This c5-b4-c3 construction, which shows up from many openings, is superb at winding down all of Black's queenside counterplay. As long as that chain holds, Black simply can't get his pawns moving.

The king walks to d2 to shepherd the c3-pawn — because you shouldn't tie a heavy piece to a menial defensive job. The rook on d8 isn't dangerous, and the king, the piece not yet participating, is the perfect defender; its home is c2.

Get the bishop out first with the move to e2, heading for f3. When Black tries the bishop to d7 and c6 for the long diagonal, White meets it on f3 — a defended square from which the bishop pressures b7.

The pawn to a4, as planned — it prepares b5 and the advance of the queenside pawn majority. Meanwhile that light-squared bishop of Black's does nothing; judge a piece by what it actually achieves, not by how many squares it nominally covers.

The rook to d6 is a classic maneuver: place one heavy piece ahead on the file to clear the way for the other. And recapture on d6 with the knight, not the pawn — the pawn recapture hands Black a tempo, and keeping the current structure leaves his knight paralysed by the weak c3-pawn.
The pawn to h3 restricts Black's pawns and denies any ...g4 activity. There's no hurry — Black isn't threatening anything — so tighten the vice before converting.

Here's the tactic that wins a second pawn: the pawn to f4 knocks the bishop off e5, and after the trade White captures on f6 with check and comes around to collect on h5. It doesn't end there — the bishop will fight back to e5, and the knight is freed by walking the king to e4 to dislodge it.

children.idea: Before the king commits to e4, fix the queenside with the pawn to c4. That's the magic of the line: after the king comes to e4 and Black tries the bishop to c3 to win the b4-linchpin of the majority, the knight jumps to f4 with check and escapes — c4 first is what makes it work.

Now it's just too many passers. The pawn to c6 creates an outside passer on the a-file — the general rule is that a passed pawn wants to be as far from the enemy pieces as possible, and corner pawns are the hardest of all to stop.

node.idea: The French, and the pawn to e5 sets up the Advance. What follows is the Nimzowitsch treatment — a dangerous line that teaches closed structures and positional chess as much as it wins games.

Instead of the automatic c3 to prop up the chain, slip through the cracks with the knight to f3 — develop as if nothing were wrong and let Black ruin the pawn chain by capturing on d4. It looks utterly counter-intuitive, and that's the point.

The bishop's best square is d3, behind the pawn. The bishop to b5 is a paper tiger — Black just blocks with the bishop to d7 — whereas from d3 it eyes h7, so if Black castles kingside a Greek-gift sacrifice is always waiting.

Black lunges with the pawn to c4, and the bishop simply steps back to e2. In a closed centre you can afford to move the same piece twice — and White has provoked c4, which relieves all the pressure on d4 and hands White a free hand on the queenside.
Now break the chain at its links: the pawn to b3 leans on c4, and the pawn to a4 will lean on b5. Classic pawn play — put pressure on both pawns at once and dismantle the structure without delay.

The pawn to a4 hits b5, the base of the chain — and note the tactical detail: the defence ...a6 is futile, because after the trade on b5 Black can't recapture with the a-pawn without hanging the undefended rook on a8. Timing is everything; strike before Black consolidates.
Take the base first — the capture on b5 removes the linchpin of the chain. Only then does the pawn on c4 fall, and with it comes a permanent structural weakness.
After the trades resolve on c4, White has achieved exactly the plan: a long-term, permanent weakness on the queenside. The c4-pawn is a chronic target that isn't going anywhere.

Castle first — it's safe, because Black has no way to get at the d4-pawn, and the knight on f3 guards e5 so a capture there is impossible. Then the pawn to c3 secures d4, and only after those preliminaries does White set about winning c4.

Black tries the pawn to f6 to open the centre — but that's counterproductive when you're behind in development, so welcome it. Capture on f6 and pry open the e-file, right onto the chronic weakness on e6.
No need to force it — the controlled move is the rook to e1, keeping the queen back to guard d4 for now. With two weaknesses on e6 and c4 and no time to develop, Black simply cannot hold.
The king came out to f7 to defend e6, but the knight to g5 forks it with check and knocks it back. The pawn is won — though there's still technique to show with the king this exposed.

Black's king walks into the pin, and the clinical punish is the rook takes e6 with check — but the check is just a bonus. The real point is that next comes the pawn to d5, winning the knight on c6 because its defender is pinned, and the whole queenside can stay home.

The pawn to d5 is the game-winner — it wins the pinned knight, and once that minor piece falls the king is hunted down. White won't even need most of the queenside pieces; the already-active ones are that powerful.

The finish is straightforward attacking chess: after the capture on c6 with check the knight defends the rook — that detail matters — and the king is dragged to c7. The bishop to f4 checks, and after the block the queen takes on d6 with checkmate.

node.idea: The pawn on c4 hands the knight a potential outpost on d4 — but there is no rush to sit on it. The knight comes to c6 first; the d4-hole is a long-term weakness that will tell only once everything is developed.
The fianchetto goes in. It concedes one thing — White can answer with the pawn to d4 and steer into a standard Maróczy Bind — but in return the g7-bishop gets a magnificent long diagonal.

With the bishop on g7 Black is already comfortably better: the dark squares in the centre are dominated, and White's light-squared bishop is stuck behind its own c4-, d3- and e4-pawns — a big pawn, not a piece.
The pawn to d6 improves the position and, more to the point, prepares to trade off the f3-knight with the bishop to g4 — the knight is White's main guard of the d4 square. The g8-knight can wait.
The bishop steps to g4, clamping down on d4 by threatening to trade the very piece that controls it. This is classic positional chess — remove the defender of the square you want.

Eliminate the knight while the chance is there. Trading the light-squared bishops is only fine for Black, but removing White's f3-knight — the guard of d4 — is the real prize, so take it now before it can slip away.
The Botvinnik setup: fianchetto plus the pawn to e6, carving out e7 as the developing square for the g8-knight. The pawns stand like teeth, gripping the central light squares White can never occupy.
The unassuming pawn to a6 is the first step of the real plan: preparing the b5 break to prise open the queenside where Black is stronger.
Now — and only now — the knight lands on d4, chosen at the most opportune moment rather than the first. It cements the grip while the queenside break is readied.
The knight to f3 with check is the clean finish — a fork that ends it at once, far quicker than grinding a simplified endgame a queen up.

node.idea: The Alekhine: Black offers the knight as a target, daring White's pawns forward. The whole opening is a provocation — let the centre advance, then strike at it.

This is the critical fork in the road. Three or four sound setups exist here; the Four Pawns Attack is the one for the player who wants to punish the Alekhine — little theory to learn, and a real chance to blow Black off the board.

The pawn to f4 completes the Four Pawns Attack — pawns on c4, d4, e4 and f4, absolute central domination. It is the most ambitious try, but it comes at the cost of development: play it carelessly and White can be crushed inside five moves.

Recapture toward the centre with the f-pawn — NOT with the d-pawn, which would invite an unfavourable queen trade. The plus of the whole system is a monster centre; the minus is lagging development, so precision is required.

The knight to c6 is the main line — and here is the pitfall: the natural knight to f3 is a mistake. It walks straight into the capture on d4 followed by the bishop pin on g4, dropping the e5-pawn. Nor does the knight to e2 help — it blocks the bishop.

The key restraint: do NOT push c5 to gain a tempo — that would concede the d5-square as a permanent outpost and tear a hole in the centre. Instead defend the e-pawn by developing the bishop to e3, keeping the whole pawn mass intact.
Develop the knight to c3. It supports the centre and readies the answer to the knight jump to b4 — the rook simply steps to c1 and the intruder achieves nothing.
Now the knight comes to f3. With enough pieces out, the pin by the bishop on g4 has lost its sting, so it is time to finish developing and think about castling.

Once Black has castled queenside, the pawn to c5 changes everything: it clamps the position and jump-starts a queenside pawn-storm straight at the black king, with the queen ready to swing out to a4 and join in.

node.idea: Black meets e4 with the pawn to e6 — the French. The plan today is aggressive: build toward the enemy king and see if the attack can land a checkmate.

The pawn goes to e5 — the Advance. This is the Steinitz treatment, a line that has been around forever but flies under the radar: the e5-pawn locks Black in and the whole game will orbit around keeping it there.
Black strikes with the pawn to c5, and here everyone and their brother plays c3 to shore up d4. Not today — giving that pawn away looks unthinkable, and that's exactly the point of the line.
Pretend nothing is happening and develop the knight to f3. The d4-pawn can fall; what matters is the e5-pawn and a fast, harmonious setup behind it.

Bishop to d3, still developing as if the centre weren't on fire — and quietly inviting Black to grab the pawn. Let him: the e5-pawn is the one really squeezing his position, so that's the pawn to nurse.
Castle and accelerate — the rook is coming to e1 not to attack yet but to over-protect e5. Leave d4 alone, pile support behind the clamp, and let development do the talking.
The knight to h6 is the standard French rerouting — it's heading for f5. Don't capture it; taking only helps Black's structure and hands him the open lines he wants.

The knight to c3 — looking deeper, this stops the ...Nb4-d6 idea that would dig at the light bishop, and it develops toward the centre. Sometimes the useful move is simply the one that denies the opponent his plan.

Here is the move to burn into memory: with a knight on c3 and the enemy queen on b6, always look at the knight to a4. It hits the queen and the c5-pawn at once, and Black's whole queenside starts to wobble.

The knight takes on c5 and the bishop recaptures — and that's the real gain. When the dust settles Black's dark-squared bishop has been traded off, White owns the two bishops, and Black's position is positionally in shambles.

No rush to attack — the pawn to c3 guards the d4-square, a very typical, solid touch, and Black's ...Ng4 is nothing to fear because the queen to e2 and a later h3 simply shove it back. Play it positionally first.
The pawn to b4 isn't just a hit on the queen — it stakes out c5 as an outpost. Every tempo now buys an important square for the pieces, and the bishop already has its eye on that hole.

The bishop swings to d6, parking itself right in Black's gut and slicing down the diagonal. There was no hurry — but with everything else in place, planting it here is a fine way to finish the buildup.

Now for the concrete phase. Development is done, the bishop dominates, and Black's king is stuck in the centre with no castling in sight — so the knight jumps to g5 and the queen heads for h5. This is going for the throat.

node.idea: Black opens with the pawn to g6 — the Modern, not a French, though it will soon take on a French-shaped centre. Against it the plan is a broad pawn chain to blunt the fianchettoed bishop.

The pawn to c3 builds the chain, so the bishop on g7 is biting on granite — it stares at d4 but can't budge it. The one downside is that c3 denies the knight its natural c3-square; no problem, the knight simply develops to d2 instead.

Just like in the London, once you've built the little pawn house you put the bishop in its hole — the bishop to d3. Try to get the dark-squared pieces sorted before that knight commits, and otherwise just develop naturally.

Black plays the pawn to d5, and closing with e5 is a no-brainer. The move to g6 already weakened all the dark squares, and shutting the centre makes those squares far easier to target — this becomes a French-style Advance with an extra hole on f6.

When Black locks it further with the pawn to c4, that suits White perfectly — the queenside is sealed, the d4-pawn is under no real pressure, and White gets what amounts to a free hand to attack on the kingside.
The attack will aim at the dark squares Black conceded — above all f6 and e5. The job now is to route the b1-knight toward those holes, and everything is arranged around getting it there.
The rook to e1 looks odd, even bad — but its purpose is to vacate f1 for the knight. The route is knight to d2, to f1, then to e3 or g4, and on toward the f6-square.
The knight came to f5, and the bishop to g5 exploits its drawback: it hits the queen with tempo along the now-open diagonal, keeps the clamp on f6, and readies the pawn to g4 to chase the knight.
Black's pawn to f6 does White's work: after the trades the e5-square becomes a gaping weakness. Occupy it with a knight, not a rook — a rook is a poor blockader — and there's no rush to do it.
The knight to e3 keeps to the plan, eyeing g4 and then the e5-outpost. Flexible, unhurried — the square isn't going anywhere.

With total control of e5 there's no need to rush a piece onto it — nobody can contest it. Connect the rooks first, maybe double on the e-file, and stay patient; here the threat is stronger than the execution.
Before anything else, stop Black's one idea — the pawn to g5. The move to h4 does it; f4 would only weaken things by cutting the queen's diagonal. The h4 and g3 arrangement locks the kingside down.

Normally you'd keep the knight on e5, but concretely the capture on g4 transforms the advantage — the knight has done its job, and now the rook simply collects the pawn on e6, leaving White up material with that monster e5-square intact.

Don't reflexively retreat the rook — marinate on the position and remember the bishop kept on c2 all game. It rakes the diagonal toward h7, and that's why the rook can crash into g6 with decisive threats. Black resigns.

node.idea: No need to rush the pawn to d5 with nothing developed yet — the simplest is to get the knight to f3. Once the pieces are out, the central breaks d5 and e5 become real; premature, they're just concrete for its own sake.

Black's pawn to d6 is another passive, unforcing choice. Play it as primitively as possible — the knight to c3, keeping it in the spirit of e4. The pawn to c4 would be reasonable, but that's really a queen's-pawn way of playing.

The bishop to d3 is the square I want: it reinforces the e4-pawn and, once Black castles, prepares the pawn to e5 with the bishop staring at h7. The queen later joins on e4 — bishop and queen aimed at h7 is a real mate threat. Note the point: even when the h-pawn moves, the square it left behind stays weak.

Castle and keep making the most standard moves — the knight jump to b4 isn't even a threat, since the bishop just steps back and a3 shoos it away. This is the dynamite: the pawn to d5. The d6- and e6-pawns are hooks, and advancing onto them forces the centre open. Two moves do the job, but only this one opens the file I actually want — the e-file, the direct path to Black's king.

Recapturing on d5 completes the operation — the e-file is open straight at Black's uncastled king, and this is exactly why castling early mattered: the rook is already home to use the file the moment it opens.

Now the objective crystallises: keep Black's king in the centre. It's hard to shoot a moving target — if the king reaches the kingside the attack restarts from zero. The rook to e1 pins the bishop the moment it appears, chaining the king to its defence.

First the bishop checks from b5, sidestepping a trade headache — and this light-squared bishop is worth keeping, because Black's pawn to b6 punched holes all over the light squares that only this piece can occupy.

The pawn to a3 shoves the knight, and you want to do this regardless of the follow-up: a minor piece parked on your side of the board is a target for pawns. It has to trudge back to a6, and now it's really out of play.

node.idea: The pawn to c5 arrives and the normal move would be c3 — but not here. The knight to f3, leaving d4, is the treatment: an idea of Nimzowitsch's whose whole purpose is to accelerate White's development.

Develop as if nothing is happening — the bishop to d3, not b5. The bishop to b5 is a very common mistake in these positions: the queenside pin is rarely dangerous, whereas from d3 the bishop points straight at the kingside where Black will castle.

Now the zen of the whole system: establish total control of the e5-square. That advanced pawn — and the piece that replaces it — is everything. Lose the grip on e5 and Black's pawns start rolling up the board; hold it and Black stays cramped.
So the rook comes to e1, reinforcing the e5-point before Black can chip at it. Rook to e1 or bishop to f4 — either adds a guard to the square the whole game revolves around.
Recapturing with the knight on e5 keeps the grip — the pawn is gone but a piece takes its place, and control of the square is unbroken.

The bishop goes to f4, and don't be seduced by the one-move pin on g5. The goal isn't a cheap pin — it's more control of e5. Even if f4 looks a touch lame, positionally it's the right call because it guards the square.

Even more control is needed, so combine two jobs in one: develop the last knight to a square where it heads for f3 and adds yet another defender of e5. Bring the undeveloped piece out and let it reinforce the battle square at the same time.

With the knight to f3 there are now so many pieces holding e5 that any single one can leave its post and the square still stands — that was the whole point. Just stay alert to the x-ray on the undefended bishop; a later drop back to g3 is the tidy prophylactic.
The capture on c6 comes with force — the recapture with the b-pawn is forced, because otherwise the queen simply hangs. That opens the way to collect on d6 next.

A textbook never-pre-move moment: the rook takes on c4 looks great, but calculate one move further — Black replies c5 and rips open a massive diagonal for the bishop, and White isn't better. Take the two seconds; the right move is the queen to d4.

The queen to d4 hits the enemy queen, and a trade there leaves Black's pawn structure in ruins. This is the typical way to convert: force the queens off into a position where the static weaknesses decide.

The move is the pawn to d5 — declining the gambit outright. It's exceedingly rare, and precisely because of that, if White isn't accurate he can end up slightly worse. This is the whole point: a practical weapon that dodges the booked-up main lines.

The natural reaction is the knight to f6, developing and steering away from a queen trade. Keeping the queens on suits the side that's better developed, and Black is happy to keep pieces on the board.

The knight to c6 hits the queen with tempo, and now precision is required. Don't leap the knight into e4 — the pawn to f3 would trap it. The clean move is the knight back to d7: it concedes the d5-pawn but keeps everything safe and coordinated.
From here it's easy conversion. The pawn to b5 kicks the bishop and Black simply grabs the central pawn, then hurries the pieces out. When you're up material, speed of development finishes the job.
The knight to c4 centralises, heading for its best square. Improving the worst-placed piece is the quiet engine of conversion.

Here's the whole roadmap: develop your pieces to active squares — the rook to c8 — then identify the biggest target and trade pieces when it doesn't harm your position. Simple, methodical, and decisive when you're already better.
